An EF-1 tornado touched down along Glade Lane and tracked east-southeast across Fox Road and through the north side of the Ruth and Bristerville communities. The tornado dissipated near the intersection of Silverton Trail and Orchard Lane, but additional straight line wind damage to trees and power lines continued south and east of the tornado path. The maximum wind speed of this tornado was 105 mph.

This tornado began near Pleasant Hill Drive and Elm Lane in southeastern Lincoln County and tracked eastward, crossing MS Highway 583 in the Ruth community. It then continued along Greenwood Road and Raiford Trail, crossing Primitive Drive in the Bristerville community, then across Monument Trail and Junction Lane before crossing into southwestern Lawrence County near the Verna community. It crossed Holmesville Road and paralleled Verna Road before lifting near Excell Boyd Road. Along the path, countless trees were snapped or uprooted, some in large swaths, multiple outbuildings sustained damage, utility poles were damaged, a mobile home sustained roof and skirting damage, and a site built home sustained minor wind damage. The maximum wind speed of this tornado was 105 mph.

This tornado began near Pleasant Hill Drive and Elm Lane in southeastern Lincoln County and tracked eastward, crossing MS Highway 583 in the Ruth community. It then continued along Greenwood Road and Raiford Trail, crossing Primitive Drive in the Bristerville community, then across Monument Trail and Junction Lane before crossing into southwestern Lawrence County near the Verna community. It crossed Holmesville Road and paralleled Verna Road before lifting near Excell Boyd Road. Along the path, countless trees were snapped or uprooted, some in large swaths, multiple outbuildings sustained damage, utility poles were damaged, a mobile home sustained roof and skirting damage, and a site built home sustained minor wind damage. The maximum wind speed of this tornado was 105 mph.

This tornado began near Junction Lane and Ard Trail in far southeastern Lincoln County, crossing Holmesville Road as it moved into far southwestern Lawrence County around Homesville Road. It continued across Woody Road, WS Cothern Road, and MS Highway 44, passing near the center of the Jayess community. It then tracked across Jessie Wallace Road and Latrell Sanders Road before lifting just north of the Walthall County line. Along the path, numerous trees were snapped or uprooted, some in large swaths. Utility poles were leaning or broken with several lines downed. Multiple homes and outbuildings sustained roof and siding damage, and a business received roof damage. A poultry farm southeast of Jayess sustained roof damage. The maximum wind speed of this tornado was 110 mph.

This tornado began near Junction Lane and Ard Trail in far southeastern Lincoln County, crossing Holmesville Road as it moved into far southwestern Lawrence County around Homesville Road. The maximum wind speed of this tornado was 110 mph.

An EF-1 tornado touched down just west of MS Highway 13 near Mapp Turner Road and moved east-southeast across Greens Creek Road, Friendship Road, Martin Bass Road, Carson-Bunker Hill Road and Hunnicut Road before crossing MS Highway 35. It lifted near Bassfield-Cemetery Road as it merged with the Choctaw Road tornado. The tornado uprooted and snapped multiple trees along the path and downed power lines. A few trees were down on a couple buildings and homes. Some tin damage was noted to some sheds and skirting was blown away from a mobile home. The maximum wind speed of this tornado was 100 mph.

An EF-1 tornado touched down along Carson Bunkerhill Road, moved east across Bass Burkett Road and Lofton Drive, and dissipated as it crossed MS Highway 35. A few trees were snapped, but most trees were uprooted along the path. A couple power lines were down as well. The maximum wind speed of this tornado was 90 mph.

An EF-1 tornado touched down near the intersection of Williamsburg Road and Claude Booth Road and tracked east-northeast across Good Hope Road and Willie Fortenberry Road. The tornado uprooted and snapped trees along the path. A few trees were downed on sheds. The maximum wind speed of this tornado was 90 mph.

An EF-1 tornado touched down just east of MS Highway 42, tracked east, and dissipated in Covington County near MS Highway 589. Trees were damaged along Hosey Mikell, Ridgeland, Stubbs, and Willie Buckley roads. A notable increase in intensity was seen as the tornado approached and crossed Gum Swamp Road around Fairman Lane. Hundreds of trees were snapped and uprooted in the area. Some minor damage was done to a few structures on the east side of Gum Swamp Road. The tornado continued east into Covington County at Sumrall Road where additional trees were uprooted. The tornado continued northeast and ended along MS Highway 589 where it uprooted a tree and snapped some large branches. The maximum wind speed in this tornado was 105 mph.

Golf ball sized hail fell along a swath from just north of Satartia, across Yazoo City, and ended just to the northeast of Yazoo City. This large hail was generated from a supercell thunderstorm which also produced the tornado which moved through the southern and eastern portions of Yazoo City.

Tornado initially touched down and tracked northeast through the area south of Yazoo City. At this point, the tornado was narrow and weak, with only relatively minor tree damage observed. As the tornado crossed Highway 16 on the east side of Yazoo City, it became wider and stronger. Several homes and businesses sustained roof damage along Highway 16 and Old Benton Road, and numerous trees were snapped and uprooted. The tornado maintained this strength for a number of miles as it moved northeast, snapping, splintering and uprooting a number of hardwood and softwood trees as well as downing powerlines. The tornado weakened somewhat as it crossed into Holmes County, before reintensifying again at Ebenezer Coxburg Road. Here is where the tornado reached its maximum intensity, with several homes and a church suffering significant roof damage along with swaths of trees being splintered or snapped. Winds here were estimated to be 115 mph, at the low end of EF2. The tornado then weakened again before dissipating just to the northwest of the Brozville community. The tornado had a total path length of 29 miles across Yazoo and Holmes Counties.

Sleet began to mix with rain around 715 in the Morton and Forest communities. Light rain, sleet and then snow continued for the next few hours before completely changing over to snow around 945. Light to moderate snow would continue to fall for over 2 hours with accumulations approaching 2 inches right around 12pm. Heavy snow then began with accumulations quickly piling up. By 1245 an observation just to the southwest of Morton reached 5 inches in snow accumulation. Moderate to Heavy snow would continue through 230 across portions of the county. By 130 the southwestern half of the county had reported close to 5 inches in many locations but the northeastern half had just started to get into the more moderate to heavy snow. This caused communities like Hillsboro and Sebastopol to go from just over an inch around 145 to up to 6 inches by 230pm. At that time the intensity of the snow decreased and all winter precipitation had moved out of the county by 330pm. Numerous trees, tree branches and powerlines came down due to the heavy wet snow.
A few trees were blown down near the Yazoo/Holmes county line.
Sporadic trees and large limbs blown down near the Yazoo/Holmes county border.

A swath of penny hail fell from just northwest of Goodman, across Durant to just south of West. This occurred from a supercell thunderstorm which moved across eastern Holmes County. The storm and penny sized hail continued into northwest Attala County.
A few trees were blown down along Tinsley Road.
Eighty mph wind gusts caused shingle damage to 3 homes in Durant. One home sustained significant shingle damage which led to leaks in the roof.

This tornado touched down and crossed Hendrix Road where a mobile home was heavily damaged. Half the roof and structure was destroyed, all the windows were blown out, and the windows on a nearby car were blown out. Another nearby mobile home had the skirting blown out. The tornado tracked northeast, taking the tops out of some trees along Lewis Creek Road. The tornado dissipated shortly after this point. Maximum winds were around 90 mph.
Several trees were blown down and some vehicles were damaged with broken windows and large limbs on them.
A swath of penny hail fell across the northwest portion of Attala County.
A swath of penny to quarter sized hail fell from near Yokena to Vicksburg.

The tornado track started just south of the city limits of Natchez, tracked northeast across the southeast side of the city, and then moved into unincorporated areas east of the city. Numerous hardwood and softwood trees were snapped and uprooted along the path. Around 50 homes were damaged, mostly from trees falling on them. Six commercial buildings were damaged, mainly roof damage. One power pole was snapped and power lines were down in several locations along the path. Maximum winds were around 110 mph.
A quick 2 inches of heavy rainfall flooded a few homes in Rolling Fork. The flood damage was minor in nature.
A swath of penny to quarter sized hail fell across the eastern portions of Holmes County.
Two trees were blown down along Highway 42 just northwest of Bassfield.

This tornado touched down and tracked along County Road 4106. Several homes suffered minor to moderate roof damage, and a number of trees were snapped and uprooted along the path. A couple of mobile homes had roof and siding damage and had the skirting blown out. Powerlines were downed at several locations along the path. Maximum winds were around 100 mph.
Two farm buildings were damaged and a couple trees were blown down along Highway 429.

The tornado started out in a forested area west of Hamburg. The timber damage in this area became quite intense, with swaths of pine trees snapped and leveled. As the tornado crossed Highway 33, it moved through a small community of homes, causing roof damage to a frame home and several mobile homes. Additionally, several outbuildings were destroyed, and windows were blown out of vehicles. The rest of the tornado��s path was across rural forested areas of southern Jefferson County, and damage was mainly limited to tree damage. However, one home did suffer some minor roof damage and some farm outbuildings sustained some roof damage. Maximum winds were around 105 mph. Total path length across northwest Franklin and southern Jefferson Counties was 11 miles.

The tornado started out in a forested area west of Hamburg. The timber damage in this area became quite intense, with swaths of pine trees snapped and leveled. As the tornado crossed Highway 33, it moved through a small community of homes, causing roof damage to a frame home and several mobile homes. A swath of dime to penny sized hail fell across western Clay County.

The tornado began around 2.2 miles northwest of Gallman near Lake Copiah along Sumrall Road. The main damage from this tornado was numerous large trees snapped and uprooted along the path. Maximum winds were around 86 mph.

The tornado touched down again along Dees Road just southwest of Crystal Springs. The tornado downed and damaged several trees along the path. A large tree was uprooted and fell on top of a residence along South Pat Harrison Road. The tornado was also responsible for tearing off the metal roof to a covered walkway at Crystal Springs Middle School. The tornado dissipated shortly after and no other damage was found. Maximum winds were around 82 mph.
Several trees were blown down.
Two trees were blown down.
A quick 2 to 3 inches of rain caused flooding around Vaiden. City Hall, a restaurant and a few businesses were flooded.
Penny sized hail fell across portions of southwest Rankin County.

This tornado touched down just northwest of Star along Highway 49 and tracked along Muse Road for a mile. The tornado caused extensive damage to the Star baseball field. It knocked down the light fixtures off the poles. Metal fences were blown down and the dugout structure was destroyed. Damage to a couple of cars in the area also occurred due to fallen trees. The tornado damaged a residence with an 8 foot hole to the roof and completely destroyed a well constructed metal outbuilding that housed a small personal airplane. This is where the tornado was at peak intensity with winds estimated to be around 112 mph and a rating of EF2. Most of the other damage along the path was uprooted and snapped trees. The top to a small well house was also toppled.

The tornado touched down again, in the Thomasville Community along Garrett Road. It caused extensive tree damage along Garrett Road, Shell Oil Road, Highway 18 and Cannon Drive. The tornado also crossed the southeast portion of the Robinhood Community with snapped and uprooted trees as well as downed power lines. Maximum winds were around 94 mph.
A couple trees were blown down along Brown Road.

The tornado finally touched down about 7 miles southwest of Pelahatchie, causing tree damage with snapped trees and tree limbs being the primary damage. A couple of trees were uprooted and the metal roof from an abandoned building was torn off and strewn across the neighboring field. This small location was where the tornado likely reached its peak intensity and rated EF1 with maximum winds around 86 mph.
Three trees were blown down across a road on a hunting lease.

Straight line winds, around 77 mph, occurred along a swath about 1 mile long in northwest Neshoba County along county road 602 and 802. Several trees and large limbs were blown down. This brief tornado snapped and uprooted several trees along a short path in the Arm Community. Maximum winds were around 80 mph.

Most of the damage was minor to moderate tree damage along the tornado path. However, an outbuilding was destroyed on Burrow Road, with the tin strewn dozens of yards downstream. Additionally, one house on Fate Ward Road suffered some roof damage. Maximum winds were around 95 mph.
A swath of penny to nickel sized hail across all of central Covington County.

Numerous hardwood and softwood trees were snapped and uprooted along the brief 1 mile path. Damage occurred to 1 home and an unoccupied building. The unoccupied building was the most heavily damaged with two broken windows and damage to the roof, eves, and siding. Two outbuildings were also damaged. One power pole was snapped high off the ground. A highway sign was blown over and a business sign was also turned over. Some of the trees were blown onto Interstate 59. Two motorists were injured when their vehicles were hit by the trees. Maximum winds were around 95 mph.
Quarter sized hail fell in Laurel.

Damage occurred to 7 apartment buildings. Most of the damage was to siding and to roofs. One apartment building had significant damage to the roof. Several hardwood and softwood trees were snapped, one of which fell onto an apartment building. Two cars were blown into each other and one had the windows broken. Three homes had minor shingle damage and the garage door of one home was damaged. The tornado tossed trees onto Interstate 59. Maximum winds were around 100 mph.

Several hardwood and softwood trees were uprooted and one softwood tree was snapped. Three chicken houses had some of the roof blown off and one had a section that collapsed. Nickel size hail was reported in Stringer. This hail was also reported in the Bay Springs community where a spotters yard was completely covered.

Numerous roads and streets were flooded in the city of Columbus and across portions of Lowndes county. Rainfall amounts around the county were observed to be around 5 to 6 inches with radar estimates up to 7 inches. Water was reported up to the steps of several homes in Columbus.
Several creeks in rural Clay County was reported to be out of their banks and across county roads. Radar estimated rainfall amounts to be 3 to 7 inches.

Heavy rainfall, between 2 and 4 inches, occurred across portions of eastern Leake County. High water covered portions of Highway 488 near Madden.

A weak brief tornado touched down at the intersection of highway 45 and Minnow Bucket road and traveled east northeast for almost 2 miles. Two different witnesses saw the tornado. Along the path one large tree was torn out. Numerous large limbs and pine needle debris was blown about. This tornado was rated EF0 with 75 mph winds.

The first round of heavy rain occurred during the morning hours and produced locally heavy rainfall. This cluster of storms moved through the county and caused water to cover portions of U.S. Highway 51.
A series of heavy storms which crossed the county caused portions of two roads to be closed due to high water. The roads that were closed were, College Street and Military Road.

Several clusters of heavy rain producing storms caused numerous streets to flood around Starkville. The heavy storms also caused standing water and street flooding along Yates street and near Highway 12 by the Starkville Health Department Building.

Multiple clusters of heavy rains and thunderstorms moved across most of Webster County. This rain event lasted for quite some time with multiple storms occurring from afternoon through the overnight hours. Flooding was extensive across the county with many roads flooded. Several roads were actually closed due to high water as 5 to 8 inches of rain fell across the area. A few homes were also flooded with a home around Mathiston having up to 4 feet of water in it.
Locally heavy rain fell across the northern portion of the county which resulted in several roads flooded within the community of Duck Hill and surrounding low lying areas.

Multiple clusters of heavy rain moved across the county from the afternoon through the early morning hours. Many roads were flooded across the southern portion of the county with several roads closed due to high water. Rainfall amounts between 5 and 8 inches fell across the area.

A series of thunderstorms, which produced several rounds of heavy rain, moved across the county and caused road and street flooding. This rain event lasted for a long time as multiple rounds of heavy rain caused the flooding to linger from the afternoon hours until the morning hours of the 28th.
A series of heavy storms caused several roads and portions of U.S. Highway 61 to be covered with water near downtown Cleveland. Rainfall between 2 and 3 inches fell.
Several clusters of thunderstorms and heavy rainfall caused several flooded streets in and around Ruleville. Rainfall between two and four inches fell around the Ruleville area.

Multiple clusters of thunderstorms and heavy rains caused several roads in Columbus and across the county to have water covering them. On some roads the asphalt was broken due to water. Rainfall totals between 5 and 8 inches of rain fell during this prolonged rain event.

A elevated supercell thunderstorm produced a swath of penny sized hail across all of Clay Couty from just north of Pheba, through West Point, and then continued east into northern Lowndes County.

A supercell thunderstorm caused a brief tornado near Prairie Point which touched down along Stoke Williams road. Six to eight trees along a tree line were damaged. A few trees had the tops twisted off and other trees were snapped or downed in a concentrated area. Max winds were around 73 mph.

A line of severe storms caused down trees on Ashley Road, just off Highway 461, and along East Lincoln, and Jefferson Streets in Hamburg. Numerous trees were also down on Hancock Road in North Crossett.
Pressure gradient winds behind a strong cold front caused trees|to fall on power lines near Minter City.
Numerous large limbs were blown down around West Point.
An supercell thunderstorm produced a swath of quarter to ping pong ball size hail across most of central Ashley County.
An isolated severe storm caused a swath of nickel to half dollar size hail across the southern portion of the county.
A 3rd supercell thunderstorm moved across a large portion of Ashley County and produced a swath of quarter to half dollar sized hail.

An isolated severe storm produced a swath of quarter to golf ball sized hail across northern Chicot County. This storm continued to produce large hail as it crossed the Mississippi River into Washington County.
A couple streets were flooded across South Jackson. This occurred as 2 inches of rain accumulated over 4 to 5 hours.
An isolated severe storm caused penny size hail near Minter City.
Penny sized hail fell just south of Caledonia.
Patchy light snow showers moved over the county overnight. Also area|law enforcement estimated around one half inch of light snow on grassy surfaces around the Jackson area.
Patchy light to moderate snow showers moved over the county overnight and ended prior to dawn. Greenwood reported around 1.5 inches of snowfall.

Patchy light snow showers moved over the county overnight and ended just|after dawn. A half inch of snow was reported on grassy surfaces around|Kosciusko. Bridges along highway 440 and highway 35 were iced over.
Patchy light to moderate snow showers moved over the county during the night and ended around dawn. Three inches was measured near Eupora.
Areas of light to moderate snow showers moved over the county overnight and ended by mid morning. Air Force Meteorologist and pilots reported 3 inches of snowfall at the Columbus Air Force Base.
Areas of light to moderate snow showers crossed the county overnight and ended around mid morning. Three inches of snowfall was reported in the northeast portion of the county.
Areas of light to moderate snow showers crossed the county overnight and|ended prior to dawn. An estimated 1.3 inches was observed in Cleveland.
Patchy light snow showers crossed the county overnight and ended prior to dawn. One inch of snow was observed on vehicles in Vaiden.
Patchy light snow showers crossed the county overnight and ended around|mid morning. WTOK TV observed around a half inch of snowfall in downtown|Meridian.

An isolated severe storm, which moved out of extreme northern Washington County, produced as swath of quarter size hail across southeast|Bolivar County.
An isolated severe storm caused nickel size hail in southern Washington county.

A short swath of penny sized hail fell just southwest of Natchez and across some of the City. Frequent lightning was also observed with this storm.

This tornado began near the Lauderdale-Clarke county line about one quarter of a mile from Sam Gray Road. Along the path, a roof was blown off a house and a barn was damaged. Numerous trees were blown down along the path with some trees on a church. A portion of Highway 45 was closed due to trees across the road. Maximum winds were around 95 mph.

A series of storms moved across the northern portion of Forrest county. Widespread 1 to 3 inches of rainfall was reported in the Hattiesburg area. Flooding was reported on numerous roads and streets around Hattiesburg. Three to four cars were flooded within a mile of Forrest General Hospital with a person trapped in his car from high water.
Three trees were blown down off Highway 133 near Clear Lake.
Skirting was blown out from a few mobile homes.

Multiple rounds of thunderstorms and heavy rainfall caused widespread flooding across the county. Several roads were closed during the heavy rainfall event. Rainfall totals between 5 and 8 inches fell across the county during the prolonged rain event.

Multiple rounds of thunderstorms and heavy rainfall caused widespread flooding across the county. Several roads were closed during the heavy rainfall event. Rainfall totals between 4 and 6 inches fell across the county during the prolonged rain event.
Some trees were blown down on the west side of Tallulah.

On the south side of Town, a swath of 70 to 75 mph winds uprooted and damaged several trees. A few of these trees were down on homes. The wind also damaged a few roofs as tin was pealed off. Much stronger and more damaging winds occurred on the north side of town.
Several trees were blown down along Rodney Road.

A small band of severe storms caused trees to go down on Nilor Road and power lines down on Jefferson Davis Road. Trees were also blown down on a house on Walnut Circle, Pool Road and Harrison Street.
A few trees were blown down across the railroad track. A train ran into those trees that blocked the tracks.

A swath of intense straight line winds, between 80 and 90 mph, occurred across the northern portion of town, across Highway 605, and to the Mississippi River. Several structures were damaged with minor to major roof damage. An open tractor shed had the roof torn off along with another shed. A string of 12 power lines were down with around 12 poles leaning over. One pole was snapped at the crossbow. Most of this area was open, but several trees were snapped and uprooted near the levee.

This tornado blew most of a roof off an antebellum house and caused shingle damage to 3 other homes. Several hardwood and softwood trees were uprooted and numerous limbs were snapped off. Maximum winds were around 85 mph.
Several trees were blown down with a few blocking Old Benton Road.
A few trees were blown down in the Cayuga area.
A few trees were blown down across McNair Road.

This tornado touched down just southeast of Brownsville along Lorance Road and traced east across northern Hinds County before moving into southwest Madison County. Hundreds of trees were snapped and uprooted along the path along with several power lines down. Several roads were blocked by downed trees along with Highway 49 just south of Pocahontas. Maximum winds were around 105 mph with a total path length across Hinds and Madison Counties of 12 miles.
A few trees were down across Norrell Road.

This tornado touched down just southeast of Brownsville along Lorance Road and traced east across northern Hinds County before moving into southwest Madison County. Hundreds of trees were snapped and uprooted along the path along with several power lines down. Several roads were blocked by downed trees along with Highway 49 just south of Pocahontas. Maximum winds were around 105 mph with a total path length across Hinds and Madison Counties of 12 miles.
Numerous large hardwood and softwood trees were snapped and uprooted along the path. Several homes had minor to moderate damage, mostly to roofs. Maximum winds were around 110 mph.
Several small pines were snapped and one large oak tree was uprooted. Minor shingle damage occurred to several houses. Maximum winds were around 85 mph.

Intense straight line winds occurred across the northern end of the City of Madison. Near the northern entrance to Ashbrooke Subdivision, across Catlett Road and along Quail Ridge Drive several hardwood and softwood trees were uprooted. Numerous homes had shingles missing and one had a large section of the aluminum roofing torn off. Two homes also sustained damage from uprooted trees. The swath of wind damage was almost a mile long and around 200 yards wide. Maximum winds were between 85 and 95 mph.
Several trees and a few power lines were blown down along Highway 28.
Several trees were blown down along Highway 98 across a large section of Franklin County.

Dozens of trees were uprooted and snapped in the Center Ridge and West Lincoln Communities as intense straight line winds (95 mph) occurred within a squall line. Many of these trees were down across roads, a few on homes as well as several power lines blown down. Some of the worst damage was across Jackson Liberty Road and Arlington Road.

Another portion of Lincoln County was hit by intense straight line winds along a squall line which ranged from 80 to 95 mph. Numerous trees and power lines were blown down along a swath starting a few miles south of the I-55 and Highway 84 intersection and continued generally east to the Harmony and East Lincoln Communities. Several trees were down on homes and a few chicken houses were damaged.

Numerous trees were blown down with many across roads throughout the southern portion of Adams County. Additionally, several power lines were taken down as well which resulted in 100 to 200 customers without power.
Dozens of trees and numerous power lines were blown down across a large section of central Lawrence County. Wind gusts within the squall line ranged from 70 to 85 mph.

Along the path, 60 homes were damaged or destroyed. A large, well-built church was destroyed. A warehouse was significantly damaged and a radio tower was snapped. Hundreds of hardwood and softwood trees were snapped and uprooted. The highest winds occurred at the church and nearby houses and trees just southwest of Magee along and just off Highway 28. A few trees were blown down off Prospect Cedar Lane.
A carport was blown away.

This tornado started just off of County Road 20, on private property, about 1 mile ESE of Montrose. Several trees were uprooted/snapped at this location and again just to the east along County Road 206. The tornado moved across several miles of wooded bottom land before crossing County Road 2414. Substantial damage occurred along County Road 2414, 4 homes were heavily damaged. The worst was where a home on pillars was pushed off its blocks. One quarter of the roof was heavily damaged. Numerous trees were snapped and uprooted with 2 large trees down through a mobile home. An ATV was rolled down a hill over 100 yards. The tornado then crossed Highway 503 and destroyed an old church building. The weakly fastened roof was blown off and then the walls collapsed inward. Numerous trees and several power lines snapped. Path width was around 500 yds at this point. The tornado continued to the ENE through northern Jasper County. Another home was pushed off its pillars and peeled all the tin off the roof, this occurred on County Road 24. The tornado then crossed County Road 2422 and downed many more trees, tore part of the roof off one home and damaged an old shed. Another old structure had some of the tin roof peeled off. The tornado crossed into Newton County at 2:52 am. It then crossed Griffis Fountain Road. The tornado crossed Parks Mill Road and dissipated just to the east of that point. Many trees were damaged along Parks Mill Road. The total path length across both counties was 19 miles. Maximum winds were around 110 mph.

This tornado touched down along Mason Creek Rd about 6 miles west of Soso. Several trees were snapped and uprooted and some minor roof damage occurred to a few homes. The tornado intensified as it crossed Summerland Road. Here the tornado widened to 500 yds and reached peak intensity, especially within a narrow corridor which lasted about 3/4 of a mile. One well constructed home suffered major damage with half of the roof torn off and other wall sections of that side the house ripped out and thrown into the back yard. Two well built storage buildings were destroyed with the contents thrown into a field. Additionally, a weekly built barn was destroyed with tin thrown along the path. Numerous trees were snapped and uprooted in this area with splintered trees within the most intense core. One large tree in this location was uprooted and actually thrown and rolled a small distance. The tornado continued to track just east of north across several more roads, including Highway 28 and 503, uprooting and snapping numerous trees. On the east side of Highway 28, a mobile home was pushed off its foundation and the person inside was injured. The tornado continued to weaken as it crossed Highway 503 and damaged more trees and caused minor damage to several mobile homes and heavily damaged a couple sheds. Maximum winds were around 125 mph.
A couple trees were blown down, one tree was down on a car.
A mobile home was moved and a garage door was damaged at another home. A chicken house also sustained minimal damage. This occurred as a squall line moved across the area.
A roof was peeled off a mobile home off Vimville-Causeyville Road and several trees were blown down across the southern portion of the county.

Several trees were blown down across the northern portion of the county.

This tornado touched down along Cemetery Road and tracked northeast toward the Pine Ridge Community. Several trees and large limbs were blown down along the track, along with a street sign. Tornado was visually spotted by storm spotters.
A tree was down along Highway 553, just northwest of Fayette.
Nickel size hail was observed near Tilton.
Penny to quarter sized hail fell west of Morgantown.
Trees were down across roads in the southeast portion of the county near Bassfield. Downed trees were reported also in the east portion of the county near the Covington County line.
Golf ball size hail was reported along Highway 35.
A few power lines were blown down near D'Lo.
Quarter sized hail was reported in Gatesville.
Quarter sized hail occurred just to the southeast and east of Soso.
Several trees were blown down.
A swath of penny to golf ball size hail fell across central Forrest County. The larger golf ball sized hail was reported southeast and east of Hattiesburg.
A swath of quarter to half dollar sized hail fell across a large portion of central Richland Parish.
Nickel sized hail was reported in the Carson area.
Tractor Trailer and SUV were blown into the Median on Interstate 20 in Start along with a tree on a home. Extensive tree damage with power outages occurred in and around Rayville.
A couple of trees were blown down south of Roxie.
Penny sized hail occurred just east of Shivers.
Nickel sized hail was reported at the intersection of Highway 84 bypass and Highway 51 just southeast of Brookhaven.
A couple of trees were blown down northwest of Oak Vale.
A swath of penny sized hail occurred across a large portion of Smith County, generally from Mize to Sylvarena.

Numerous trees were blown down across central Smith County, especially around the Center Ridge Community. A few trees were down on homes and one chicken house was destroyed and two others had minor damage.

Numerous trees blown down across the county. Many trees blown down on homes and cars. This was from gradient winds from a wake low passage. Wind gusts look to have been around 50 mph and were from the southeast.

Numerous trees were down around the county with many across roads and some city streets. Power outages were scattered across the city of Columbus as well as in the county. This was due to gradient winds from a Wake Low passage. Winds were estimated around 50 mph.

A swath of wind damage occurred across a large portion of west-central, north and northeast Jasper County. As a fast moving squall line entered the county, a few trees were blown down just south of Louin, 3 were down across Highway 15. Numerous other trees were blown down near and east of Montrose and across the north and northeast portion of the county. Several of the downed trees in this portion of the county were across roads.
Numerous trees down across the southeast portion of the county, especially on Griffis Ferris road and Beason road. Trees were also down along Highway 503 south of Hickory.
Numerous trees were blown down across the south portion of the county.
Several trees were knocked down across the county. This was from gradient winds from a wake low passage. Wind gusts were around 50 mph and were|from the southeast.
Several roads were flooded east of Brookhaven from heavy rainfall.

Widespread 3 to 4 inches of rain brought significant flooding to most of the county. Cars were inundated with two feet of water over roads in multiple locations and water covered Highway 11 in Purvis. In Sumrall, water flooded City Hall along with several other streets and roads around that area.
Heavy rain, between 2 and 3 inches, caused the intersection of Cooper Road and Highway 472 to flood.

Multiple rounds of storms brought 3 to 4 inches to a large portion of Forrest County. This heavy rain caused numerous streets and roads around Hattiesburg to flood. Over a foot of water was reported on Highway 49 near the University of Southern Mississippi.

Multiple rounds of storms caused serious flash flooding across central and southern portions of the county. People were trapped in houses on Henderson Canal Road. Fire Dept had evacuated people by boat. Water had covered portions of several roads. In Columbia, water was close to entering a few stores on Main Street. Rainfall totals ranged between 3 and 5 inches which fell in 5 to 6 hours.
Several rounds of storms produced widespread 2 to 4 inches of rain. This caused numerous streets around Laurel to flood and several other roads across the county.
Several county roads were flooded around D'Lo as 2 to 4 inches of rain fell across the area.
Penny size hail occurred around Baskin.
Nickel size hail occurred northwest and north of Clayton.

A swath of quarter to half dollar size hail fell across all of southern Lamar County. The half dollar sized hail caused minor damage to a truck just southwest of Baxterville. Nickel size hail was reported in Baxterville, and just south of Purvis along the swath.
A swath of nickel to golf ball size hail fell across southern Forrest County. Golf ball sized hail was reported in the Paul B. Johnson state park. Nickel size hail was reported in the Carnes area.
Several trees were reported down on the north side of Cocodrie Lake.
Penny size hail was reported in Improve.
Pea to penny size hail was reported in Puckett.
The swath of at least quarter sized hail continued into the southern portion of Concordia parish.
A swath of penny to quarter size hail occurred across a large portion of central Lamar County.

This tornado briefly touched down and damaged 4 homes with minor to moderate damage mainly to roofs. One home had a deck and back portion of the house ripped off. A couple of sheds were also destroyed with numerous hardwood and softwood trees snapped and uprooted. The tornado moved along County Road 94 until it lifted as that road intersected with Highway 37. Maximum winds were around 100 mph.
A swath of penny sized hail occurred across a portion of northwest Jasper County.
A portion of a roof was blown off a barn.
Wind gusts between 65 and 70 were reported from Meehan to Meridian. Several trees were also blown down.
Numerous trees were down across the western portion of the county to central sections.
Several inches of rain caused a good portion of Lower Brookhaven Road to flood.
Heavy rainfall, between 3 and 4 inches, caused several roads to flood around Bassfield. Some of the roads had as much as 2 feet of water covering the roadway.
A swath of quarter size hail fell across a large portion of Richland Parish. This hail occurred from southwest of Alto to near Mangham.
The observer also noticed gusty winds of unknown velocity.
Trees and a powerline were down in Crowville.
A swath of quarter sized hail fell across the central portions of Bolivar County, which included Mound Bayou.
A swath of quarter sized hail was observed on the south side of Brookhaven, which included some nickel sized hail on Zetus Road southwest of Brookhaven.
A large tree blocked a road about one mile south of Wesson.
A swath of quarter sized hail fell around Florence and Brandon. Penny sized hail fell at Pellhatchie.
Golf ball size hail was reported west of Ruth.
Quarter size hail was spotted at Topeka school.
A swath of quarter to half dollar sized hail fell across a large portion of southern and central Leake County, generally from Lena to near Edinburg.
Quarter inch hail was observed near the Branch Community and on Highway 13 just north of Forkville.
Penny sized hail fell in Morton and near Roosevelt State Park near Interstate 20.
Nickel size hail was spotted on Highway 80 west of Forest.
A few trees were blown down near Eupora.
Several trees and power lines had blown down west of Columbia.
Hail was measured to be nickel size in diameter just west of Arlington.
Power lines and several trees were blown down along Highway 503 and areas just south of Decatur. Five trees were blown down just north of Little Rock.
Two trees were spotted down just east of Conehatta.

Half dollar to golf ball size hail damaged vehicles at Oktibbeha County lake. Quarter sized hail fell west of Starkville on Self Creek Road. Quarter sized hail was observed at the intersection of old Highway 12 and Newlight Road. A car windshield was damaged.
A few trees were blown down east of Montrose.
A swath of quarter sized hail occurred across a large portion of Clay County, generally from the southwest portions to the northeast areas.
Several trees and power lines were blown down across northeast Clay County.
A few trees and a power line were blown down in and around Lumberton.
A few trees were blown down with one large tree on a house which caused major damage.
A few trees were blown down in Meridian.
A few trees and power lines were blown down along with a tree on a trailer.
Several trees and a few power lines were blown down across East Hattiesburg.
A few trees were blown down at Tuckers Crossing.
A couple of trees were blown down around the city, one had fallen on a house.
A few trees were blown down.
An estimated wind gust of 70 mph was observed along Highway 8.
A swath of penny to quarter sized hail fell across central Chicot County and through the south side of Lake Village.
Tops of rotted trees fell on two houses in Lake Village.
A large tree was uprooted on Main street in Indianola.
Down trees were discovered along Highway 82 east of Greenwood Airport. A tree fell on a house near the highway.

A downed tree was discovered in the middle of the road along highway 7 west of Grenada. A tree was noted on Scenic Road north of Grenada. Wind|had blown a sign into a car on Interstate 55 around the Highway 7 exit. A downed tree was sighted on Cecil-Shelton road in Grenada.
Trees were discovered blown down across the Natchez Trace Parkway along with other downed trees on Highway 15.
Four hundred and fifty people had a power outage due to downed trees on power lines north of Ackerman.
Fifteen hundred customers had power outages due to numerous downed trees on power lines across Clay County. A power pole was snapped and numerous trees were blown down near the Monroe County line.
Two trees were blown down in Columbus.
A swath of penny to quarter sized hail fell across a portion of central Simpson County.

The tornado tracked across rural southern Ashley County and snapped and uprooted hundreds of large hardwood and softwood trees. Forty two homes were damaged with approximately 15 homes that were heavily damaged or destroyed. The most intense damage was along Meridian Church Road in southwest Ashley County. Here, intense tree damage resulted in several cross roads being blocked by dozens of trees, and several mobile homes and houses were destroyed by the winds and fallen trees. This was the area rated EF2 with 130 mph winds. Over the last several miles of the track, the tornado was narrower and damage was primarily in the EF1 category.

A swath of nickel to golf ball sized hail fell across a large portion of central Ashley County. Golf ball sized hail occurred around Crossett as this supercell storm, the one which produced the EF2 tornado in the southern portion of the county, tracked east.
Penny size hail fell in Wilmot with some possibly larger stones.
A few downed trees damaged some roofs around Wilmot.
A few trees were blown down around Eudora.
A swath of quarter to hen egg sized hail occurred across all of southern Chicot County as a supercell storm tracked east.

A swath of penny to nickel sized hail fell across all of Richland Parish, generally along I-20, as a supercell storm tracked east. Nickel sized hail was observed between Start and Rayville in the Girard Community. Penny sized hail was spotted around Rayville.

The tornado appeared to have started along I-20, just west southwest of Delhi, and it downed a few trees. As the tornado passed just south of Delhi, shingles and roofing were taken off the roof of a couple of apartment buildings and several trees were downed. The tornado then crossed I-20 and entered western Madison Parish. A few more trees were blown down before it dissipated. Maximum winds were around 90 mph.
Strong gradient winds, behind a fast moving line of showers, damaged 2 metal building doors along with a large billboard.
A roof had pealed off a shop on Laughlin Road between Boyle and Cleveland.
Several trees and large limbs were discovered downed around Greenwood on Highway 7 and Grenada Boulevard.

Numerous downed trees were observed across the northern portion of the county, some of which fell on roads including Highway 51. A mobile home was pushed off its blocks and damaged west of Sweatman. A few other homes were damage some by wind and others by trees in the same area.
Quarter sized hail was observed at Eagle Lake.
A few trees were blown down around the Clarkson Community.
Quarter to golf ball sized hail was observed in northern Lowndes county.
A few trees were blown down around the Caledonia area.

A swath of quarter to half dollar sized hail was observed across a large portion of central Ashley County. The swath of hail was from just southwest of Crossett to northeast of Hamburg. The hail damaged some windshields near Crossett.

The tornado appeared to have started along I-20, just west southwest of Delhi, and it downed a few trees. As the tornado passed just south of Delhi, shingles and roofing were taken off the roof of a couple of apartment buildings and several trees were downed. The tornado then crossed I-20 and entered western Madison Parish. A few more trees were blown down before it dissipated. Maximum winds were around 90 mph.
A swath of penny to quarter sized hail fell across all of Madison Parish as a supercell storm tracked east.
A swath of quarter sized hail fell across central portions of Chicot County. The hail swath went through Lake Village where quarter sized hail was observed.
A swath of quarter sized hail fell across a portion of central Sunflower County.
A roof sustained damaged and some trees and power lines were blown down across Cleveland. Winds occurred from a gravity wave feature as a large moderate rain shield was moving through the area.
Five to 10 trees were snapped and uprooted just south of Deer Park.
A home was struck and damaged occurred to many electrical appliances.
A few trees were blown down across eastern Adams County.
A couple trees were blown down.
A couple of trees were blown down off Highway 98.

Strong easterly winds developed as the back edge of the rain shield pushed east in response to a wake low and rapidly falling pressures. Wind gusts between 40 and 50 mph downed a few trees across Madison County. A couple of these trees were down across roads.
Several trees were blown down along with a few power poles broken off. This damage occurred along Highway 51 just south of Brookhaven.

Strong easterly winds developed as the back edge of the rain shield pushed east in response to a wake low and rapidly falling pressures. Wind gusts between 50 and 60 mph downed several trees across portions of Leake County. A couple of these trees were down across roads.

Strong easterly winds developed as the back edge of the rain shield pushed east in response to a wake low and rapidly falling pressures. Wind gusts between 50 and 60 mph downed dozens of trees across Attala County. A few trees were down across area roads.

Strong easterly winds developed as the back edge of the rain shield pushed east in response to a wake low and rapidly falling pressures. Wind gusts between 40 and 50 mph downed a few trees along with a highway sign.

Strong easterly winds developed as the back edge of the rain shield pushed east in response to a wake low and rapidly falling pressures. Wind gusts between 50 and 60 mph downed several trees across Choctaw County. A few trees were down across area roads.

Strong easterly winds developed as the back edge of the rain shield pushed east in response to a wake low and rapidly falling pressures. Wind gusts between 50 and 60 mph downed dozens of trees across Winston County. A few trees were down across area roads.
Numerous trees and some power lines were blown down across the central portion of the county as wind gusts between 70 and 80 mph blew through.
Numerous trees fell south of Rockport, which blocked some roads.

Numerous streets and roads were flooded around Monticello, including the downtown area. Oak Grove Church Road just outside of Monticello had portions of it washed out. The Sheriff's office discovered that a car had driven into a washed out road. Also numerous roads across the county had flooded.

Strong easterly winds developed as the back edge of the rain shield pushed east in response to a wake low and rapidly falling pressures. Wind gusts between 50 and 60 mph downed dozens of trees across Newton County. A few trees were down across area roads.

Strong easterly winds developed as the back edge of the rain shield pushed east in response to a wake low and rapidly falling pressures. Wind gusts between 50 and 60 mph downed dozens of trees across Neshoba County. Some trees were down across area roads.

Strong easterly winds developed as the back edge of the rain shield pushed east in response to a wake low and rapidly falling pressures. Wind gusts between 50 and 60 mph downed dozens of trees across Oktibbeha County. Some trees were down across area roads.

Strong easterly winds developed as the back edge of the rain shield pushed east in response to a wake low and rapidly falling pressures. Wind gusts between 50 and 60 mph downed dozens of trees across Lowndes County. Some trees were down across area roads and power lines. One tree was on a house near Caledonia.

Strong easterly winds developed as the back edge of the rain shield pushed east in response to a wake low and rapidly falling pressures. Wind gusts between 50 and 60 mph downed several trees across Clay County.
Trees were knocked down on Highway 37 near the Smith-Covington county line.

Strong easterly winds developed as the back edge of the rain shield pushed east in response to a wake low and rapidly falling pressures. Wind gusts between 50 and 60 mph downed several trees across Noxubee County.
Several reports of an estimated 70 mph winds were observed between Collins and Seminary.

Strong easterly winds developed as the back edge of the rain shield pushed east in response to a wake low and rapidly falling pressures. Wind gusts between 50 and 60 mph downed several trees across Kemper County.

Strong easterly winds developed as the back edge of the rain shield pushed east in response to a wake low and rapidly falling pressures. Wind gusts between 50 and 60 mph downed several trees across Lauderdale County. A measured wind gust of 56 mph was recorded at Key Field in Meridian.
A few trees were blown down just west of Heidelberg along County Road 31.

Numerous roads were flooded across rural parts of the county and in Prentiss. Vehicles were flooded on Highway 13 and one vehicle went off into a flooded creek. Prentiss fire department measured 4.20 inches of rain with 1.32 inches in one hour. Rainfall totals ranged from 4 to 6.5 inches across the county.

Extensive flash flooding was observed across most of Lincoln County, especially in the southern part of the county. Numerous roads were flooded, included were a few that do not typically get flooded. One person had to be rescued on Summit Road near the Pike County line. Rainfall totals ranged from 4 to 6 inches.
A number of trees were blown down across the southern part of the county.

Widespread flash flooding occurred across Covington County as 4 to 6.5 inches of rain fell. Water covered Mcdonald Road just south of Collins. Water washed out culverts on Deerman Road just south of Collins. Numerous other roads were flooded across the county. A portion of Highway 49 was covered with high water for a short period of time. Sanford recorded 4.8 inches of rain. A half inch fell in ten minutes.

About 13 downed trees were observed from Interstate 59 to the Perry County line. The area was mainly in a line from the Glendale community to the Macedonia and Sunrise communities. An outbuilding had the tin roof torn off. Some trees and power lines were also blown down just north of Petal along Highway 42.

Strong easterly wind gusts, between 50 and 60 mph, developed across the southern portion of Morehouse Parish as a wake low evolved across the region. These high winds downed several trees and power lines.

Strong easterly wind gusts, between 50 and 60 mph, developed across West Carroll Parish as a wake low evolved across the region. These high winds downed numerous trees and power lines. Some trees were down on homes with others across area roads.

Strong easterly wind gusts, between 50 and 60 mph, developed across East Carroll Parish as a wake low evolved across the region. These high winds downed many trees and a few power lines. A couple trees were also blown down across area roads.
Widespread heavy rain, between 4 and 6 inches, flooded several roads throughout the county.
Strong easterly wind gusts, between 50 and 60 mph, developed across Issaquena County as a wake low evolved across the region. These high winds downed several trees with a few down across area roads.

Strong easterly wind gusts, between 50 and 60 mph, developed across Sharkey County as a wake low evolved across the region. These high winds downed dozens of trees and several power lines. One home sustained minro shingle damage from the high winds.

Strong easterly wind gusts, between 40 and 50 mph, developed across the southern portion of Washington County as a wake low evolved across the region. These strong winds downed a few trees and large limbs. In Hollandale, one tree fell on a house and caused damage.
Strong easterly wind gusts, between 40 and 50 mph, developed across the southern portion of Sunflower County as a wake low evolved across the region. These strong winds downed a few trees.

Strong easterly wind gusts, between 40 and 50 mph, developed across the Humphreys County as a wake low evolved across the region. These strong winds downed a few trees. In Isola, a playhouse was destroyed and car was damaged by a large limb.
Strong easterly wind gusts, between 40 and 50 mph, developed across the Holmes County as a wake low evolved across the region. These strong winds downed a few trees.

Shears Road flooded in the northeast portion of the county along with several other roads. Rainfall amounts between 4 and 7 inches occurred across portions of the county with 6.7 inches measured in Sumrall.

Strong easterly wind gusts, between 40 and 55 mph, developed across the Leflore County as a wake low evolved across the region. A 53 mph wind gust was measured at the Greenwood-Leflore Airport. These strong winds downed a few trees.

Strong easterly wind gusts, between 40 and 55 mph, developed across the Carroll County as a wake low evolved across the region. A 53 mph wind gust was measured at the Greenwood-Leflore Airport. These strong winds downed a few trees.
Strong easterly wind gusts, between 40 and 50 mph, developed across some of Warren County as a wake low evolved across the area. These strong winds downed several trees.

Strong easterly wind gusts, between 40 and 50 mph, developed across some of Richland Parish as a wake low evolved across the area. These strong winds downed several trees where a few downed some power lines.

Widespread flash flooding occurred as 4 to 6.5 inches of rain fell across the county. Many roads were flooded across the county with several washed out. A portion of Highway 29 was undermined and was closed for a period of time. Additionally, numerous streets were flooded in and around Laurel.

Numerous roads were flooded in Hattiesburg, which almost flooded some homes. Numerous roads were flooded in the northern portion of the county around Highway 42. Several roads were washed out as well across the northern sections. Rainfall totals ranged from 4 to 6 inches.
A swath of penny to quarter sized hail fell across the southern portion of the county. This was a left moving supercell which continued into Lamar County.
A swath of penny to quarter sized hail fell across portions of western Lamar County. This occurred from the same left moving supercell storm which came out of southern Marion County.
Quarter inch sized hail was discovered near Rawls Springs.
Nickel sized hail was spotted near New Hebron.
Quarter sized hail was observed just southeast of Martinville.
A swath of penny to quarter sized hail fell across western Smith County.
A couple trees were blown down along Highway 18 and Martin Lane just west of Raleigh.
A few downed trees were observed along Holly Grove-Meeks Road.
A swath of quarter to hen egg sized hail occurred over a portion of northern Holmes County, along Emory Road. At least one home had the windows busted out by wind driven hail.

A swath of golf ball to baseball sized hail was observed. Many vehicles were damaged with dents and windows broken out. Trees were damaged as well by the hail with tree branches broken and leaf debris all around the Black Hawk community.
Several trees were blown down near the Oma Community.
Numerous signs blown down and at least two awnings blown off a business. Numerous trees and limbs blown down in the Belzoni area along with a tree on a house.
A swath of nickel to walnut sized hail fell across all of central Humphreys County.
A swath of quarter to walnut sized hail fell across all of Holmes County as a supercell thunderstorm tracked east.
A few power lines were blown down from large broken tree branches.
A few trees were blown down east of Lexington.
A few downed trees were observed across some roads north of Durant.
A swath of quarter sized hail fell across all of the northern portion of Attala County as a supercell thunderstorm tracked east.
A swath of quarter sized hail fell across a portion of central Humphreys County between Midnight and Silver City.
A swath of nickel sized hail occurred across the western portion of Attala County and this was observed in the Possumneck Community.
Sixty mph winds were estimated in the Possumneck Community.
A few trees were blown down with several large limbs. Young corn stalks were flattened by the wind gusts just south of Thorton.
A swath of quarter sized hail fell from near Weir to Ackerman.
Walnut sized hail fell northeast of Bastrop as a swath of hail fell across all of central portions of Morehouse Parish.
An 18 wheeler was blown into a ditch as well as some downed trees southeast of Beekman.
Numerous trees and power lines had blown down across the parish, mainly between Oak Grove and Pioneer.

Tree debris was discovered in a yard along with skirting blown out from a mobile home. Siding from a mobile home was pushed out and a tree was blown down on a workshop. This occurred along Oil City Road. Several trees has their tops broken and twisted out.
A few trees were blown down along Adams Street.

This tornado touched down along Mt Zion Road near the Madison/Leake County line and tracked into Leake County to just southwest of Thomastown. A number of downed trees along the patch including a few across Damascus Church Road. Total path length was around 4 miles across both counties.

This tornado touched down along Mt Zion Road near the Madison/Leake County line and tracked into Leake County to just southwest of Thomastown. A number of downed trees along the patch including a few across Damascus Church Road. Total path length was around 4 miles across both counties.
Downed trees were discovered south of Singleton on Highway 35.
Two pine trees and one oak had snapped off in the same direction at the residence of a retired NWS employee.

Along Road 179, a structure sustained wind damage with shingles from a house blown off and tin from a shed removed. Also, a mobile home had major damage and another home had minor damage due to downed trees outside Philadelphia.
A few power lines were spotted down around Shuqualak.

A narrow tornado downed a number of trees along its path. This weak tornado downed a large tree across the access road to Sicily Island Wildlife Management Area near the start of the path. Other downed trees were across State Highway 913, just before the tornado dissipated. Maximum winds were around 70 mph.
Large limbs were knocked down around Wisner. New corn crops had leaned as a result of the strong winds.
Thunderstorms caused widespread downed power lines and trees across the parish. Downed trees was observed in the Sandy Lake community, between Jonesville and Harrisonburg.
Downed trees were spotted near Waterproof. Several trees had blown down and the tin was blown off the roof of a business around St Joseph.
Numerous downed trees observed between Vidalia and Ferriday and across central portions of the parish.
Scattered trees were blown down just northwest of Prentiss to near Highway 13.
Several trees were blown down and snapped around Taylorsville.
Several roads were flooded across the central and southern portion of the county as 4 to 6 inches of rain fell.
Many roads were flooded along with several washed out across the central portions of Forrest County. Heavy rainfall between 4 and 6 inches fell in a short time and caused all the flooding problems.
A swath of penny to quarter sized hail fell across central Adams County, including in and around Natchez.

Significant wind damage occurred across a large portion of Adams County. Winds were rated as high as 80 to 90 mph with a large bowing segment of a progressive derecho. Hundreds of trees and numerous power lines were downed across the county. According to Emergency Manager, 41 structures were damaged across the county. Structural damage was a mix of major to minor and were mostly damaged by fallen trees, but many were also damaged by the intense winds.

The tornado started along Russum Westside road, snapping and downing a number of trees and large limbs along the road. The tornado then crossed Old Colony Road, downing several trees and large limbs across the road. The weakening tornado then crossed the Natchez Trace Parkway and US Highway 61, downing a few trees and large limbs, before dissipating. Maximum winds were around 90 mph.
Quarter sized hail was spotted at Russum and across portions of western Claiborne County.
Many trees and power lines were blown down across the northern half of Jefferson County. Highway 552, east of Lorman, was blocked due to downed trees.
A swath of penny to quarter sized hail fell across all of central Franklin County from Roxie to Meadville and Bude, as well as locations just to the east of Bude.
Several trees were blown down off Highway 61 on the north side of Vicksburg.
Fifty plus trees were blown down along a swath from around Barlow to Crystal Springs as a significant bow echo, called a derecho, raced across the area.
Numerous trees and power lines were blown down across the northern portion of the county. A few trees were down on some homes with one on a vehicle.
Several trees were blown down across central and southern portions of Hinds County. A few trees were down across area roads from just west of Raymond to around Terry.

Numerous trees and a few power lines were blown down across the northern half of Lawrence County. A few trees were down on a couple homes and some minor roof damage occurred to a few buildings in Monticello.
Many roads were covered by water in the northern portions of the county, especially in the Ponderosa, Woodyard and Westgate Communities. A few homes were inundated by high water.

The tornado began and tracked across rural northeast Jefferson Davis County, far northwest Covington County and then into southeast Simpson County. Snapped and uprooted large hardwood and softwood trees occurred along the path. The most intense damage occurred in the Saratoga Community in southeast Simpson County. A travel trailer was completely destroyed and two chicken houses were heavily damaged. Snapped pine trees fell on a church and damaged a roof and some shingle damage occurred on a few other homes. Skirting was blown off of a mobile home and a chicken house was damaged near the Simpson and Smith county line. Maximum winds were 100 mph. The track began three miles north of Clem and ended four miles north northeast of Mount Olive. Total path length across the 3 counties was around 9 miles.

This tornado touched down just south of Mt. Olive and tracked generally northeast into southeast Smith County near Taylorsville. Along the path, numerous trees were uprooted and snapped. A tree fell on a house just south of Mt. Olive and several signs were downed and a TV antenna was bent. Several houses also received shingle damage. The total path was around 20 miles with maximum winds around 100 mph.
Scattered trees were blown down across a large portion of central Simpson County as a large bow echo, called a derecho, raced across the area.

Numerous trees and power lines were blown down across the northern section of the county. The damage resulted in numerous power outages. Many trees were down across roads with a couple down on homes. This damage occurred as a large bow echo, called a derecho, raced across the region.
Lightning struck a house in the Ross Barnett Reservoir area.

Numerous trees and power lines fell across the county. There were also lots of minor roof damage to homes, especially in the Hot Coffee area. This damage occurred as a large bow echo, called a derecho, raced across the area.
An interstate sign was blown down along the eastbound lane of I-20 about one half of a mile west of the downtown Brandon exit. Power lines were blown down in the Robinhood Community.
Numerous trees were blown down across the southern portion of Smith County. Several trees were down across area roads including Highway 28 near Mize and Highway 37 near Taylorsville.

Trees were blown down along County Road 10 near Stringer and County Road 17 north of Stringer and one tree fell on a house. Trees and power lines were observed down in Stringer. Damage also occurred to a chicken house.

This tornado began 4 miles east of Taylorsville, tracked northeast into western Jasper County, and ended 1.7 miles northwest of Stringer. Maximum winds were around 100 mph, with a total path length around 5 miles. A chicken house was destroyed and another damaged. Roof damage occurred to a mobile home and a shed. Numerous pines were snapped and some oak trees were blown down.

This tornado began 4 miles east of Taylorsville, tracked northeast into western Jasper County, and ended 1.7 miles northwest of Stringer. Maximum winds were around at 100 mph, with a total path length around 5 miles. A chicken house was destroyed and another damaged. Roof damage occurred to a mobile home and a shed. Numerous pines were snapped and some oak trees were blown down.

An EF1 tornado began 3.1 miles northeast of Stringer and ended 3.7 miles northeast of Stringer. Maximum winds of 105 mph. Path length of 0.6 miles and width of 0.1 miles. Numerous large pines were uprooted or snapped.

Numerous trees and power lines were blown down across the northern part of the county. One tree fell on a house. A motorcyclist was injured when they ran into a tree which was down across a road just northeast of Laurel. This occurred as a large bow echo, called a derecho, raced across the region.

Numerous trees and power lines were blown down across the central portion of Jones County. Just east of Laurel, a woman was killed when a tree fell onto her mobile home. This damage occurred as a large bow echo, called a derecho, raced across the region.

This tornado touched down just south of Mt. Olive and tracked generally northeast into southeast Smith County near Taylorsville. Along the path, numerous trees were uprooted and snapped. A tree fell on a house just south of Mt. Olive and several signs were downed and a TV antenna was bent. Several houses also received shingle damage. The total path was around 20 miles with maximum winds around 100 mph.

The tornado began and tracked across rural northeast Jefferson Davis County, far northwest Covington County and then into southeast Simpson County. A narrow path of primarily tree damage paralleled Highway 1 from just southwest of Benoit, through Benoit, to just northeast of town. The tornado started along Levee Road and moved north-northeast snapping and downing several trees. As it crossed Highway 1, several more trees were snapped, a couple outbuildings were destroyed, and a couple of mobile homes were damaged. One framed house sustained shingle damage in this area as well. The tornado continued to the north-northeast and moved into a mobile home complex along Key Road. Here the tornado narrowed and reached its maximum intensity with winds around 110 mph. One mobile home was completely destroyed and this is where a fatality occurred. Two other mobile homes were rolled and moderate damage was sustained to several other mobile homes in the complex. In total, 3 mobile homes were destroyed and 16 damaged. A number of trees and several power lines were also blown down along the rest of the path. The tornado dissipated as it crossed Highway 438 where several large limbs were broken off trees.

This weak tornado started along Coker Road where it downed several trees along with some large limbs. The tornado also blew down a fence, a power line and caused some minor damage to a barn. At least one home was damaged by a large section of a tree which fell on the corner of the home. The tornado then tracked east northeast across Moss Ridge Road where more trees were downed along with some damage to a few fences. From there, the tornado moved across Lake Lorman and downed more trees and a power line along Lakeshore Drive. The tornado dissipated shortly after this point. This tornado was rated EF0 with maximum winds around 70 mph.

The tornado started along James Road, where several chicken houses were significantly damaged, including one collapsing. Other outbuildings were damaged and a number of trees and power lines were downed. Debris was carried for hundreds of yards along the path. The tornado traveled northeast, and reached its maximum intensity and width as it crossed Monticello Road. Hundreds of trees in this area were snapped or uprooted, including a number of large hardwoods. Convergence in the damage path was very apparent here. A barn was leveled and at least two power poles were snapped. A couple of other outbuildings were heavily damaged. The tornado continued northeast from there, crossing Perrett Road and Highway 472. Numerous trees continued to be snapped and uprooted along its path, and several outbuildings were damaged or destroyed. The tornado dissipated shortly after crossing Highway 472. This tornado was rated an EF2 with maximum winds of 115 mph.

The same parent supercell thunderstorm spawned a second path of tornadic damage to the northwest of the first tornado. This tornado started along Clifton Road, where a number of pine trees were topped and several others were snapped or uprooted. The tornado tracked northeast across Tadpole Road, where numerous trees were snapped and uprooted, including several large hardwood trees downed across the road itself. The tornado dissipated as it crossed Clifton Hillsboro Road. It was determined to be an EF1 with maximum sustained winds of 100 mph.

In addition to the damaged structures, hundreds of trees were snapped and uprooted along with many power lines taken down. The damage across this part of Warren County was in the EF2 range with maximum winds around 130 mph.

The tornado moved into Issaquena County from Warren County and mainly tracked across forested portions of the county. The tornado did track across US Highway 61 just a couple miles south of Valley Park. Thousands of trees were snapped and uprooted along the path with one abandoned agricultural building destroyed. The tornado had EF2 intensity with 130 mph winds across Issaquena County.

The path of the tornado clipped the far southeast corner of Sharkey County in the Delta National Forest. Considerable damage occurred to the timber along the path as it moved into western Yazoo County. The tornado reached EF2 intensity before moving into western Yazoo County with peak winds around 130 mph.

The tornado moved out of extreme southeast Sharkey County and into west central Yazoo County and gained intensity as it tracked northeast. The tornado caused significant home damage northwest of Satartia, and again as it crossed Highway 3 near the Crupp Community. The tornado then moved through a rural area southwest of Yazoo City, causing major damage or destruction of a number of homes, as well as intense tree damage.  As the tornado approached the intersection of US Highway 49 and Highway 16, on the south side of Yazoo City, it reached its widest point and maximum intensity. Here the rating peaked at EF4 with maximum winds around 170 mph. The tornado had a maximum width of 1.75 miles. Several buildings, including a church and several businesses, were totally destroyed. The tornado continued moving through residential areas on the southeast side of Yazoo City, heavily damaging or destroying numerous homes.  The tornado continued northeast through rural northeastern Yazoo County before it tracked into Holmes County.||A total of four fatalities occurred in Yazoo County. All of the fatalities were individuals who were in mobile homes.

The tornado continued northeast into rural southern Holmes County, causing intense tree damage and damaging or destroying a number of rural residences. The damage across this area was in the EF3 range. As the tornado moved by the Franklin Community, in rural Holmes county, it again reached EF4 intensity. It completely destroyed two brick homes and heavily damaged or destroyed a number of other homes. The tornado then crossed Interstate 55, causing significant tree damage and blowing a number of vehicles off the road. As the tornado approached the area just south of Durant and crossed US Highway 51, it narrowed and reached one of its weakest points. One fatality occurred in Holmes County.

The tornado then moved into western Attala County from just east of Durant in Holmes County. The tornado re-intensified somewhat and began causing significant tree damage in rural western Attala County. The tornado continued across Attala County, causing tree and power line damage,and heavily damaging a number of rural residences, including in the community of Hesterville. The tornado continued to the northeast and crossed the Natchez Trace Parkway. Here numerous trees were damaged and thrown across the Parkway. The maximum intensity in Attala County was EF2 with maximum winds around 130 mph.

The tornado moved into Choctaw County and crossed Black Road around 128 pm. Here, minor damage occurred to a brick home. Tree damage in this area was more substantial and was in the upper EF2 range. Thousands of trees were uprooted and snapped. Many trees were also splintered in this area. The tornado then crossed Highway 413, just east of French Camp. The tornado reached high end EF3 intensity at this point and produced significant structural damage to a number of structures. Wind speeds ranged from 155 to 165 mph at this location. Three well built brick homes were nearly flattened with only 1 outer wall left standing. Other well built structures sustained major damage to the roof. The Crossroads Grocery was destroyed as the cinder-block structure collapsed on itself. Several vehicles were thrown in this area including at semi-truck. A cell tower was snapped in half. The intense damage continued along the track across Stuart-Weir Road and White Road. Several more structures were severely damaged or destroyed in this area along with significant devastation to timber. Along Pisgah and Dotson Roads, some of the most severe damage occurred and this was the location of the 5 fatalities. Here, dozens of mobile homes and conventional foundation homes were destroyed. Multiple vehicles were thrown with a few landing in trees. The widest part of the tornado was in this general area where it was 1.07 miles wide. The EF3 intensity damage occurred for about 4 miles. The tornado weakened as it tracked toward the Chester Community and crossed Weir-Salem Road and Chester-Mills Road. Here the damage was mostly tree damage with a dozen of homes or so receiving minor to major damage. Some homes had a small portion of roof torn off or shingles peeled away. One well built home was shifted off the foundation with a portion of the back of the home collapsed. Again, timber damage was significant with a large area of pine forest heavily damaged. EF2 damaged was noted there. The tornado continued through Chester and toward Highway 9 and Highway 15. Here mainly EF1 tree damage occurred. The only exception was at and just to the east of the intersection with Highway 9 and Highway 790. Here some low end EF2 tree damage was noted. The tornado then crossed Highway 15 and continued just along and to the south of Macedonia Road. EF1 tree damage occurred in this area as well. The tornado continued into Oktibbeha County just east of of the Reform-Sturgis Road.

The tornado moved into west-central Oktibbeha County and tracked along Big Creek Road and Simmons Road before dissipating at Sturgis-Maben Road about 5 miles north of Sturgis. Many trees were snapped and uprooted as the long-track tornado came to an end.

The initial damage where the tornado developed was limited to some minor tree damage along Buddy Odom Road. The tornado tracked north northeast and rapidly became strong, with EF2 and low end EF3 damage occurring along the rest of the path. The tornado affected Shiloh and Buddy Odom Roads as well as State Highway 429 in Leake County; and County Roads 4022, 4033, 4126, 4045, 4171, 4142 and State Highway 14 in Attala County. Several mobile homes, including at least two double wides, were completely destroyed at several locations along the path, with debris carried well away from the remains. Impressive tree damage occurred at numerous locations along the path, including a couple of locations where some debarking/denuding was noted. Vehicles were rolled or tossed at several locations. A frame home was pushed off its foundation and a number of frame homes suffered moderate to major roof damage. Numerous power poles were snapped along the path. The widest point of the damage path was around a quarter mile, and was near Highway 14 in Attala County. Maximum winds were around 140 mph. Total path length across Leake and Attala Counties was 10 miles.
